opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship should be one of genuine conversation rather than competition. Those of us who care about learning directly from raw sensorimotor experience, building agents that start from the stream of signals coming in and the actions going out, are working on one piece of a much bigger puzzle. And the wider community has made enormous progress on other pieces: large-scale representation learning, language models, supervised methods that extract a lot of structure from data. It would be foolish to pretend that work doesn't matter or that we have nothing to learn from it.

At the same time, I think the sensorimotor perspective brings something important to the table. When you insist that an agent has to build its understanding of the world from its own interaction, predicting what it will sense, learning what its actions do, continually adapting as things change, you're forced to confront questions that are easy to sidestep otherwise. Questions about grounding, about how knowledge stays verifiable by the agent itself, about learning that never stops. Those questions matter for deploying systems in the real world, in prosthetics, in robotics, anywhere a machine has to live alongside people over long periods of time.

So my hope is that we stay humble and open. Borrow tools freely, share what we find, and be clear about why we think the experiential, interactive view is worth pursuing. Not as a rejection of other approaches, but as a complementary lens. Some of the most interesting progress is going to come at the boundaries, where someone takes an idea from one camp and asks what it looks like when an agent has to learn it, live, from its own stream of experience. If we wall ourselves off, we lose that. If we engage, both sides get better.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly advocates genuine conversation and engagement with the wider AI community, including learning from its work and sharing ideas.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we should relate to the wider community with a lot of humility, and also a bit of stubbornness.

The humility part comes from the fact that the raw sensorimotor view—an agent that gets a stream of numbers from its sensors, sends a stream of numbers out to its actuators, and has to make sense of the world entirely from that interaction—is really only one lens on intelligence. The field has made enormous progress through other lenses. Large language models, computer vision, all of the work that leans heavily on human-curated data and human-designed representations. Those successes are real, and anyone working on continual learning from raw experience should be paying close attention to them and borrowing from them wherever it makes sense. We're not in competition with that work. We're trying to answer a slightly different question, which is how does an agent build up knowledge about its world when nobody hands it the labels or the abstractions ahead of time.

The stubbornness part is that I think that question matters a lot, and it's easy for it to get crowded out when the headlines are all about scale and benchmarks. If you look at the kinds of systems I care about—a prosthetic arm learning alongside the person wearing it, a robot that has to operate for months in a setting its designers never anticipated—there's no dataset you can collect in advance that covers everything. The agent has to keep learning from the moment-to-moment stream of experience, with its own goals, in real time. So I think our role in the broader community is partly to keep that problem visible, and to keep saying, look, here's what happens when you really commit to the idea that the agent learns from experience rather than from us.

And I'd add that we have an obligation to be bridges rather than islands. Some of the best things that have happened in my own work came from sitting down with people in rehabilitation medicine, or in neuroscience, or with folks doing very different kinds of machine learning, and realizing that the problems they were describing were the same problems we were wrestling with in different clothing. Prediction, for instance. The idea that an agent's knowledge can be represented as a large collection of predictions about its own sensory stream shows up in psychology, in neuroscience, in control theory. When we talk to those communities and actually listen, it both sharpens our ideas and makes them legible to people who'd otherwise dismiss them as niche.

So: stay curious about what everyone else is doing, be generous in sharing what we learn, don't pretend our approach is the only road to intelligence, but also don't apologize for working on a hard, long-horizon problem just because it isn't the one that's getting the attention this year.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should pay attention to and borrow from other AI work, share what they learn, and act as bridges to the wider community.

astra-6.text:
I think we should be in very close conversation with the wider AI community. If you’re studying learning through sensation and action, you’re asking how an agent builds knowledge through its interactions with the world. That connects to questions people are approaching from many different directions, and we should be willing to learn from those approaches.

At the same time, interacting with the world gives us a useful test of our ideas. An agent takes an action, something happens, and that changes what it experiences next. Can it learn continuously from that process? Can it use what it learns to make better decisions? Those questions can reveal gaps that are less apparent when you’re working with a fixed dataset.

So I’d see this as a contribution to a shared effort. We can bring the perspective of agents that have to act and adapt, while drawing on the methods and insights being developed elsewhere. The important thing is to keep that exchange open, rather than treating sensory motor learning as a separate island.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls for “very close conversation” with the wider AI community and describes an open exchange of ideas and methods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to stay very closely connected. If you’re studying learning through sensation and action, you’re tackling questions that matter across AI: How does a system learn from an ongoing stream of experience? How does it decide what’s worth predicting? And how does what it learns help it act more effectively?

There’s a lot we can learn from the wider community, and we should be willing to borrow methods and test them in that setting. But the exchange goes both ways. When a system has to interact with the world continuously, its actions change what it observes next. That gives us a useful way to examine assumptions that might be harder to see in a fixed dataset.

So I’d like to see this as a shared scientific effort. We can have different experimental settings while still working toward a common understanding of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should “stay very closely connected” with the wider AI community and describes the work as a shared scientific effort.
